title: Unit tests, fakes & useful assertions
summary: Prove a small behavior with deterministic inputs and observable outcomes.
explanation: A unit test exercises a focused behavior without unnecessary infrastructure. Arrange establishes inputs, Act performs the operation, and Assert checks the result. Fakes provide lightweight behavior; mocks can verify interactions when those interactions are the actual contract. TimeProvider and explicit dependencies keep time, randomness, and external I/O controllable.
why: Fast deterministic tests catch regressions early and make a business rule's edge cases concrete enough to discuss.
useCase: A spaced-review scheduler gets a fixed clock. Tests prove that a wrong answer schedules a short retry and that repeated correct answers never exceed the maximum review interval.
whenToUse: Use unit tests for algorithms, rules, and meaningful error cases. Use integration tests for SQL translation, HTTP routing, or dependency wiring. Do not mock every internal method just to reproduce the implementation in a test.
pitfalls: Tests that depend on today's date or Thread.Sleep.
Asserting only that a result is non-null when the behavior is more specific.
Mocking an ORM query provider and assuming the real SQL will work.
bestPractices: Name tests after the behavior and condition.
Cover boundaries and failure paths, not only the happy path.
Prefer outcome assertions unless an interaction is the required behavior.
takeaways: A test should fail when the intended behavior breaks.
Control time and external effects instead of waiting.
The smallest useful test boundary is not always a single method.

interview.question: Mock versus fake?
interview.answer: A fake supplies a lightweight working implementation. A mock usually configures responses and verifies expected interactions. Use the least complicated double that expresses the behavior being tested.

interview.question: What makes a unit test good?
interview.answer: It is deterministic, focused on observable behavior, fast enough to run often, and capable of failing for a meaningful regression. Coverage percentages alone do not establish assertion quality.

quiz.question: A test depends on a subscription expiring tomorrow. Prefer:
quiz.explanation: A controlled clock makes boundary behavior deterministic without real waiting.

quiz.question: What should a rejected withdrawal test assert besides the exception?
options: The exact private method call order
quiz.explanation: The important invariant is that an unsuccessful operation does not alter the account balance.

title: Integration tests & real boundaries
summary: Test the wiring, persistence, and HTTP behavior that isolated tests cannot prove.
explanation: Integration tests exercise components working together. ASP.NET Core's WebApplicationFactory hosts the application for HTTP tests. Relational database tests catch translation, constraints, and transaction behavior that an in-memory object store cannot reproduce. Browser tests validate the rendered user workflow and interactions on top of these lower layers.
why: Correct classes can still be wired incorrectly. A passing mocked repository test does not prove that a SQL query translates or another user's records stay inaccessible.
useCase: An API test creates an order, fetches it as its owner, then verifies another user cannot retrieve it. A SQLite test checks that replaying the same quiz submission does not create duplicate history.
whenToUse: Use HTTP tests for routing, validation, security, and serialization. Use the production database engine, often through Testcontainers, for provider-sensitive queries. SQLite is appropriate when SQLite is the actual target; it is not a perfect SQL Server substitute.
pitfalls: Sharing mutable test data across parallel tests.
Replacing authentication in tests and never testing the real security configuration.
Using EF InMemory to prove relational constraints or SQL translation.
bestPractices: Give each test isolated data and deterministic setup.
Cover unauthenticated, forbidden, not-found, and successful responses.
Use a small number of browser tests for critical end-to-end paths.
takeaways: Integration tests verify contracts between real components.
Match the database engine when provider behavior matters.
Browser tests prove interaction, not just server status codes.

interview.question: Why not use EF InMemory for every persistence test?
interview.answer: It is not a relational database and does not reproduce SQL translation, relational constraints, or transaction behavior. Choose SQLite for a SQLite app, or use the actual engine for engine-sensitive behavior.

interview.question: What does WebApplicationFactory add?
interview.answer: It boots the ASP.NET Core application in a test host with configurable services and an HttpClient, allowing tests across routing, middleware, serialization, and application behavior.

quiz.question: Which test best proves a uniqueness constraint for a SQLite app?
options: A real isolated SQLite database test
A test of a string constant
quiz.explanation: The actual relational engine enforces the constraint and exposes its real failure behavior.

quiz.question: A good ownership test should include:
options: A second user trying the same resource ID
quiz.explanation: Cross-user attempts expose object-level authorization and data-isolation failures that the happy path misses.

title: Structured logging & observability
summary: Leave enough context to explain a failure without logging sensitive data.
explanation: Structured logs separate a stable message template from values so fields can be searched and aggregated. Metrics summarize numerical behavior; traces connect spans across a request and its dependencies. Log levels communicate significance. Correlation identifiers tie events to one operation, while OpenTelemetry provides standard instrumentation and export conventions.
why: Production issues rarely reproduce on demand. Good observability makes it possible to distinguish a slow dependency, invalid input, and a code defect with evidence.
useCase: An order request carries a trace ID through HTTP and database work. Logs include order ID and outcome, metrics track error rate, and a trace shows where latency accumulates without exposing a customer's payment details.
whenToUse: Log important state transitions and unexpected failures at the responsible boundary. Use metrics for rates and distributions, traces for causal timing, and logs for detailed events. Avoid storing request bodies by default.
pitfalls: Interpolating strings and losing structured fields.
Logging passwords, tokens, cookies, or payment details.
Logging the same exception at every layer and creating noise.
bestPractices: Use named placeholders and useful event context.
Choose levels intentionally and control production verbosity.
Set retention and access rules for telemetry data.
takeaways: Stable templates preserve searchable structured fields.
Logs, metrics, and traces answer complementary questions.
Telemetry needs privacy and retention boundaries.

interview.question: Why use placeholders instead of interpolation?
interview.answer: A template such as Order {OrderId} preserves a named field for structured providers and groups related events by a stable template. Interpolation turns values into an opaque rendered string before logging.

interview.question: Logs versus traces?
interview.answer: Logs describe discrete events. Traces connect timed spans across the path of one operation, helping explain dependency relationships and where latency occurred. Both can share trace identifiers.

quiz.question: Which log statement best preserves an OrderId field?
quiz.explanation: A named placeholder separates the template and value, allowing structured providers to retain the OrderId field.

quiz.question: What should not be logged as routine request context?
quiz.explanation: Tokens are credentials. Logging them can expose accounts through telemetry access or retention.

title: CI/CD & production-minded delivery
summary: Make every change reproducibly buildable, testable, and deployable.
explanation: Continuous integration runs automated checks when changes are proposed or merged. Continuous delivery keeps a releasable artifact ready; continuous deployment automatically promotes passing changes to production. A pipeline normally restores dependencies, builds, tests, and publishes. Deployment also includes configuration, database evolution, health checks, and rollback planning.
why: A project that only works on one laptop is difficult to collaborate on. Reproducible checks expose missing files, environment assumptions, and regressions before release.
useCase: A GitHub Actions workflow restores a .NET solution, runs tests in Release, and publishes the web application. A Docker image mounts persistent SQLite storage instead of losing progress when the container is replaced.
whenToUse: Set up CI early, even for a solo project. Deploy server-hosted Blazor to a host that runs ASP.NET Core; GitHub Pages is static hosting and cannot run the .NET server or SQLite database.
pitfalls: Committing secrets, bin/obj output, or a user's local database.
Assuming a successful build means migrations or deployment are safe.
Giving workflows broad write permissions they do not need.
bestPractices: Use least-privilege workflow permissions and dependency updates.
Publish an artifact from the tested revision.
Document environment variables, data persistence, backups, and rollback constraints.
simpleCode:
dotnet restore
dotnet build --configuration Release --no-restore
dotnet test --configuration Release --no-build
dotnet publish src/Fieldnotes --configuration Release --no-build
practicalCode:
name: build
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with:
          dotnet-version: '10.0.x'
      - run: dotnet restore
      - run: dotnet test --configuration Release --no-restore
takeaways: CI proves a change builds and passes checks in a clean environment.
A deployment includes configuration and durable data, not just binaries.
GitHub can host the source; a server app needs an application host.

interview.question: Continuous delivery versus deployment?
interview.answer: Delivery keeps a tested release ready for promotion, which may require approval. Deployment automatically releases qualifying changes to production. Both depend on trustworthy checks and operational safeguards.

interview.question: What should a deployment rollback consider besides code?
interview.answer: Database schema compatibility, data changes, configuration, queued messages, and shared contracts. Rolling back binaries alone may be unsafe after an incompatible schema migration.

quiz.question: Can GitHub Pages run a Blazor Server app with SQLite?
options: Only if the repository is public
quiz.explanation: Interactive server rendering requires a running ASP.NET Core process. Static hosting cannot execute that backend.

quiz.question: Which file should normally stay out of source control?
quiz.explanation: Personal runtime data does not belong in the source repository. Commit schema and content definitions instead.
